nodes.label: Label sides of right-angled triangle
nodes.description: Label the sides of a right-angled triangle as the hypotenuse, opposite or adjacent side with respect to a given angle.

nodes.label: Write sin, cos, tan ratios
nodes.description: Write down the sine, cosine and tangent of an angle in a right-angled triangle as ratios of its hypotenuse, opposite and adjacent sides.

nodes.label: Write reciprocal ratios
nodes.description: Write down the reciprocal ratios cosecant, secant and cotangent of an angle, both as 1 over sin, cos or tan and as ratios of the sides of a right-angled triangle.

nodes.label: Evaluate sin, cos, tan on calculator
nodes.description: Use a calculator in degrees mode to evaluate sin, cos and tan of an angle, alone or inside an expression with a coefficient, fraction, power or root, correct to 2 decimal places.

nodes.label: Evaluate reciprocal ratios
nodes.description: Evaluate cosec, sec and cot of an angle on a calculator by first writing each as the reciprocal of sin, cos or tan, correct to 2 decimal places.

nodes.label: Test trigonometric statements
nodes.description: Substitute given angle values into a trigonometric statement and use a calculator to determine whether the statement is true or false.

nodes.label: Solve simple trigonometric equations
nodes.description: Solve for the unknown angle in a simple equation involving a trigonometric ratio, using the principles of solving equations and a calculator.

nodes.label: Special angle ratio values
nodes.description: State the values of sin, cos and tan for the special angles 30°, 45° and 60°, in surd form, without a calculator.

nodes.label: Ratios from surd triangles
nodes.description: Determine a trigonometric ratio of an angle in a right-angled triangle whose sides are given in surd form, using the Theorem of Pythagoras where needed, and give the answer in surd form.

nodes.label: Verify identities with special angles
nodes.description: Show that a trigonometric identity holds by substituting the values of special angles.

nodes.label: Bounds from the definitions
nodes.description: Explain, from the definitions of sine, cosine and tangent, why sin and cos cannot exceed 1 and whether tan has a maximum value.

nodes.label: Finding lengths using ratios
nodes.description: Calculate unknown side lengths in right-angled triangles by choosing the appropriate trigonometric ratio (sine, cosine or tangent) for the given angle, rearranging the equation and using a calculator.

nodes.label: Finding angles using inverse ratios
nodes.description: Determine unknown angles in right-angled triangles by writing the trigonometric ratio of the known sides and using the inverse sine, cosine or tangent function on a calculator.

nodes.label: Solving trigonometric equations
nodes.description: Solve trigonometric equations for an angle when no triangle is shown (rearranging first, converting sec, cosec or cot to cos, sin or tan where needed, and stating no solution when the ratio is out of range), and evaluate trigonometric expressions for given angles with a calculator.

nodes.label: Angle from point coordinates
nodes.description: Calculate the angle between the line from the origin to a point and the x-axis, using the point's coordinates as the opposite and adjacent sides and tan (or sin or cos), and give the angle in standard position when the point lies in the second quadrant.

nodes.label: Ratios of a point (x;y)
nodes.description: Calculate the trigonometric ratios (sin, cos, tan, cosec, sec, cot) of the angle for a point (x;y) in the Cartesian plane, by finding r with the theorem of Pythagoras and substituting x, y and r, without a calculator.

nodes.label: Ratios from a given ratio and quadrant
nodes.description: Use a sketch, the CAST diagram and the theorem of Pythagoras to decide which trigonometric ratios are positive or negative in each quadrant and, from a given ratio and the quadrant (or range) the angle lies in, determine the other trigonometric ratios, a missing coordinate or side length, and the value of expressions (including squared ratios), without a calculator.

nodes.label: Special angle ratio values
nodes.description: Determine the values of sin, cos and tan for the special angles 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90° without a calculator (including tan 90° being undefined), and use them to evaluate expressions.

solution: We first find the opposite and adjacent sides with respect to $\hat{P}$ and $\hat{R}$ : $p$ is the opposite side to $\hat{P}$ and the adjacent side to $\hat{R}$ $q$ is the hypotenuse $r$ is the adjacent side to $\hat{P}$ and the opposite side to $\hat{R}$ We also note that: $\sin\theta=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$ $\cos\theta=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$ $\tan\theta=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}$ Looking at each of the given ratios we can see that only $\cos\hat{P}=\dfrac{r}{q}$ is correct.

solution: Sarah first needs to identify the hypotenuse, opposite and adjacent sides in the triangle. content.text_md: Given the following triangle: [figure] Label the hypotenuse, opposite and adjacent sides of the triangle with respect to $\theta$ . State which sides of the triangle you would use to find $\sin\theta$ , $\cos\theta$ and $\tan\theta$ . Label the hypotenuse, opposite and adjacent sides of the triangle with respect to $\alpha$ . State which sides of the triangle you would use to find $\sin\alpha$ , $\cos\alpha$ and $\tan\alpha$ .

Label the triangle: First find the right angle, the hypotenuse is always directly opposite the right angle. The hypotenuse never changes position, it is always directly opposite the right angle and so we find this first. The opposite and adjacent sides depend on the angle we are looking at. The opposite side relative to the angle $\theta$ is directly opposite (as the word opposite suggests) the angle $\theta$ . Finally the adjacent side is the remaining side of the triangle and must be one of the sides that forms the angle $\theta$ . [figure]

Complete the trigonometric ratios: Now we can complete the trigonometric ratios for $\theta$ : $\begin{aligned}\sin\theta&=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac{CB}{AC}\\\cos\theta&=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac{AB}{AC}\\\tan\theta&=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}=\frac{CB}{AB}\end{aligned}$ Therefore to find $\sin\theta$ we would use sides $CB$ (opposite side to $\theta$ ) and $AC$ (hypotenuse). To find $\cos\theta$ we would use sides $AB$ (adjacent side to $\theta$ ) and $AC$ (hypotenuse). To find $\tan\theta$ we would use sides $CB$ (opposite side to $\theta$ ) and $AB$ (adjacent side to $\theta$ ). And then we can complete the trigonometric ratios for $\alpha$ . For angle $\alpha$ the opposite and adjacent sides switch places (redraw the triangle above to help you see this). Notice how the hypotenuse is still $AC$ . $\begin{aligned}\sin\alpha&=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac{AB}{AC}\\\cos\alpha&=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac{CB}{AC}\\\tan\alpha&=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}=\frac{AB}{CB}\end{aligned}$ Therefore to find $\sin\alpha$ we would use sides $AB$ (opposite side to $\alpha$ ) and $AC$ (hypotenuse). To find $\cos\alpha$ we would use sides $CB$ (adjacent side to $\alpha$ ) and $AC$ (hypotenuse). To find $\tan\alpha$ we would use sides $AB$ (opposite side to $\alpha$ ) and $CB$ (adjacent side to $\alpha$ ).

Use the definitions of the trigonometric ratios to answer the following questions: Explain why $\sin\alpha\le1$ for all values of $\alpha$ .

The sine ratio is defined as $\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$ . In any right-angled triangle, the hypotenuse is the side of longest length. Therefore the maximum length of the opposite side is equal to the length of the hypotenuse. The maximum value of the sine ratio is then $\frac{\text{hypotenuse}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=1$ .
Use the definitions of the trigonometric ratios to answer the following questions: Explain why $\cos\alpha$ has a maximum value of $\text{1}$ .

The cosine ratio is defined as $\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$ . In any right-angled triangle, the hypotenuse is the side of longest length. Therefore the maximum length of the adjacent side is equal to the length of the hypotenuse. The maximum value of the cosine ratio is then $\frac{\text{hypotenuse}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=1$ .
Use the definitions of the trigonometric ratios to answer the following questions: Is there a maximum value for $\tan\alpha$ ?

The tangent ratio is defined as $\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}$ . Since the opposite and adjacent sides can have any value (so long as the length of the side is less than or equal to the length of the hypotenuse), there is no maximum value for the tangent ratio.
Solve for $\alpha$ : $3\sec\alpha=\text{1.4}$ .

Convert $\sec$ to $\cos$: There is no “ $\sec$ ” button on the calculator and so we need to convert $\sec$ to $\cos$ so we can find $\alpha$ . $\begin{aligned}3\sec\alpha&=\text{1.4}\\\frac{3}{\cos\alpha}&=\text{1.4}\end{aligned}$

Rearrange the equation: We need to rearrange the equation so that we have $\cos\alpha$ on one side of the equation. $\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\cos\alpha}&=\text{1.4}\\3&=\text{1.4}\cos\alpha\\\frac{3}{\text{1.4}}&=\cos\alpha\end{aligned}$

Calculate the unknown lengths in the diagrams below: [figure]
For all of these we use the appropriate trigonometric ratio or the theorem of Pythagoras to solve. To find $a$ and $b$ we use $\cos\theta=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$ :
$\begin{aligned}\cos30^{\circ}&=\frac{a}{16}\\a&=16\cos30^{\circ}\\&\approx\text{13.86}\text{cm}\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned}\cos25^{\circ}&=\frac{b}{\text{13.86}}\\b&=\text{13.86}\cos25^{\circ}\\&\approx\text{12.56 cm}\end{aligned}$
To find $c$ we use $\sin\theta=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$ :
$\begin{aligned}\sin20^{\circ}&=\frac{c}{\text{12.56}}\\c&=\text{12.56}\sin20^{\circ}\\&\approx\text{4.30}\text{cm}\end{aligned}$
To find $d$ we use $\cos\theta=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$
$\begin{aligned}\cos50^{\circ}&=\frac{5}{d}\\d\cos50&=5\\d&=\frac{5}{\cos50^{\circ}}\\&\approx\text{7.78}\text{ cm}\end{aligned}$
Next we use the theorem of Pythagoras to find the third side, so we can use trig functions to find $e$ :
$\begin{aligned}(\text{5})^{2}+(\text{7.78})^{2}&=\text{85.5284}\\\sqrt{\text{85.5284}}&\approx\text{9.25}\end{aligned}$
We use $\tan\theta=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}$ to find $e$ :
$\begin{aligned}\tan60^{\circ}&=\frac{\text{9.25}}{e}\\e\tan60^{\circ}&=\text{9.25}\\e&=\frac{\text{9.25}}{\tan60^{\circ}}\\&\approx\text{5.34}\text{ cm}\end{aligned}$
Next we use the theorem of Pythagoras to find the third side, so we can use trig functions to find $f$ and $g$ :
$\begin{aligned}(\text{5.34})^{2}+(\text{7.78})^{2}&=\text{89.0044...}\\\sqrt{\text{89.0044...}}&\approx\text{9.44}\end{aligned}$
We use $\tan\theta=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}$ to find $g$ :
$\begin{aligned}\tan80^{\circ}&=\frac{\text{9.44}}{g}\\g\tan80^{\circ}&=\text{9.44}\\g&=\frac{\text{9.44}}{\tan80^{\circ}}\\&\approx\text{1.66}\text{ cm}\end{aligned}$
And finally we find $f$ using the theorem of Pythagoras:
$\begin{aligned}f^{2}&=(\text{9.44})^{2}-(\text{1.65})^{2}\\f&=\sqrt{\text{86.39}}\\&\approx\text{9.29}\text{cm}\end{aligned}$
The final answers are: $a=\text{13.86}$ , $b=\text{12.56}$ , $c=\text{4.30}$ , $d=\text{7.78}$ , $e=\text{5.34}$ , $f=\text{9.29}$ and $g=\text{1.66}$ .

$P\left(-3, 4\right)$ is a point on the Cartesian plane with origin $O$ . $\theta$ is the angle between $OP$ and the positive $x$ -axis. Without using a calculator, determine the value of: $\cos\theta$ $3\tan\theta$ $\frac{1}{2}\text{cosec}\theta$
Sketch point $P$ in the Cartesian plane and label the angle $\theta$: [figure]
Use the theorem of Pythagoras to calculate $r$: $\begin{aligned}r^{2}&=x^{2}+y^{2}\\&=(-3)^{2}+(4)^{2}\\&=25\\\therefore r&=5\end{aligned}$ Note $r$ is positive as it is the radius of the circle.

Substitute values for $x$ , $y$ and $r$ into the required ratios: We note that $x=-3$ , $y=4$ and $r=5$ . $\cos\theta=\dfrac{x}{r}=\dfrac{-3}{5}$ $3\tan\theta=3\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right)=3\left(\dfrac{4}{-3}\right)=-4$ $\dfrac{1}{2}\text{cosec}\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{r}{y}\right)=\frac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{5}{4}\right)=\dfrac{5}{8}$

$X\hat{O}K=\theta$ is an angle in the third quadrant where $X$ is a point on the positive $x$ -axis and $K$ is the point $\left(-5, y\right)$ . $OK$ is $\text{13}$ $\text{units}$ . Determine, without using a calculator, the value of $y$ . Prove that ${\tan}^{2}\theta+1={\sec}^{2}\theta$ without using a calculator.
Sketch point $K$ in the Cartesian plane and label the angle $\theta$: [figure]

Use the theorem of Pythagoras to calculate $y$: $\begin{aligned}r^{2}&=x^{2}+y^{2}\\y^{2}&=r^{2}-x^{2}\\&=(13)^{2}-(-5)^{2}\\&=169-25\\&=144\\y&=\pm12\end{aligned}$ Given that $\theta$ lies in the third quadrant, $y$ must be negative. $\therefore y=-12$

Substitute values for $x$ , $y$ and $r$ and simplify: $x=-5$ , $y=-12$ and $r=13$ . LHS $\begin{aligned}{\tan}^{2}\theta+1&={\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)}^{2}+1\\&={\left(\frac{-12}{-5}\right)}^{2}+1\\&=\left(\frac{144}{25}\right)+1\\&=\frac{144+25}{25}\\&=\frac{169}{25}\end{aligned}$ RHS $\begin{aligned}{\sec}^{2}\theta&={\left(\frac{r}{x}\right)}^{2}\\&={\left(\frac{13}{-5}\right)}^{2}\\&=\frac{169}{25}\end{aligned}$ Therefore the LHS = RHS and we have proved that ${\tan}^{2}\theta+1={\sec}^{2}\theta$ .

claims.claim: In a right-angled triangle, the side opposite to the right-angle is labelled the hypotenuse.
With respect to an angle θ in a right-angled triangle, the side opposite θ is labelled "opposite".
With respect to an angle θ in a right-angled triangle, the side next to θ is labelled "adjacent".
In a right-angled triangle the three sides are named according to how they are placed in relation to the angle θ.
Either non-90° internal angle of a right-angled triangle can be chosen, and the adjacent and opposite sides are then defined accordingly.
The hypotenuse remains the same regardless of which internal angle is being referred to.
The hypotenuse is always opposite the right-angle and is always the longest side.
The definitions of opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse are only applicable when working with right-angled triangles.
To label the sides, first find the right angle; the hypotenuse is directly opposite the right angle and is found first because it never changes position.
The opposite and adjacent sides depend on the angle being looked at.
The opposite side relative to the angle θ is the side directly opposite the angle θ.
The adjacent side is the remaining side of the triangle (after the hypotenuse and the opposite side) and must be one of the sides that forms the angle θ.
For the other angle α, the opposite and adjacent sides switch places compared with θ.
In the worked example the hypotenuse is still AC when the angle considered is α instead of θ.
The ratios of similar triangles are used to define the trigonometric ratios.
It does not matter what the lengths of the sides of the triangles are: if the angle remains constant, the ratio of the sides will always yield the same answer.
That triangle ABC is similar to triangle DEF is written △ABC ||| △DEF.
In similar triangles ABC and DEF, ratios between corresponding sides are equal: AB/BC = DE/EF, AB/AC = DE/DF and AC/BC = DF/EF.
In similar triangles ABC and DEF, AB/DE = BC/EF = AC/DF.
In similar triangles ABC and DEF, the angle at vertex A equals the angle at vertex D, the angle at vertex B equals the angle at vertex E, and the angle at vertex C equals the angle at vertex F.
The order of letters for similar triangles is very important: similar triangles are always labelled in corresponding order, so △ABC ||| △DEF is correct but △ABC ||| △DFE is incorrect.
The three trigonometric ratios of an angle are sine (sin), cosine (cos) and tangent (tan).
sin θ = opposite / hypotenuse.
cos θ = adjacent / hypotenuse.
tan θ = opposite / adjacent.
The trigonometric ratios relate the lengths of the sides of a right-angled triangle to its interior angles.
"Soh Cah Toa" is a mnemonic technique for remembering the trigonometric ratios sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse and tan θ = opposite/adjacent.
Always check that the triangle has a right-angle before using the trigonometric ratios, otherwise the answer will be wrong.

Each of the three trigonometric ratios (sin, cos, tan) has a reciprocal.
The reciprocal ratios are called cosecant (cosec), secant (sec) and cotangent (cot).
cosec θ = 1 / sin θ.
sec θ = 1 / cos θ.
cot θ = 1 / tan θ.
The reciprocal ratios can also be defined for any right-angled triangle in terms of its sides.
cosec θ = hypotenuse / opposite.
sec θ = hypotenuse / adjacent.
cot θ = adjacent / opposite.
sin θ × cosec θ = 1.
cos θ × sec θ = 1.
tan θ × cot θ = 1.
Cosecant may also be abbreviated as csc.

Theorem of Pythagoras: the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the two other sides.
The lengths of the sides of a right-angled triangle must obey the Theorem of Pythagoras.
Unknown lengths in right-angled triangles are found by using the trigonometric ratios.
The hypotenuse is always the side opposite the right angle, and it never changes position.
The opposite side is the side opposite the angle we are interested in, and the adjacent side is the remaining side.
To find an unknown length, first identify the opposite and adjacent sides and the hypotenuse with reference to the given angle.
sin θ = opposite / hypotenuse.
cos θ = adjacent / hypotenuse.
tan θ = opposite / adjacent.
Writing the sine ratio for the given 50° angle, with unknown side x and the hypotenuse 100, gives the equation sin 50° = x/100.
When the unknown length x is divided by a known side, rearrange by multiplying both sides by that known side: sin 50° × 100 = x, so x = 100 sin 50°.
After rearranging, use a calculator to find the answer: x = 100 sin 50° = 76.60444..., which rounds to 76.60.
When asked to round to two decimal places, the final length is written with the approximately-equal sign, for example x ≈ 76.60.
The book writes the decimal mark as a comma, for example 76.60444...
Writing the cosine ratio for the given 25° angle, with adjacent side 7 and unknown hypotenuse x, gives the equation cos 25° = 7/x.
When the unknown length x is in the denominator, first multiply both sides by x: x cos 25° = 7.
Then divide both sides by cos 25° to isolate x, giving x = 7 / cos 25°.
Using a calculator, x = 7 / 0.90630... = 7.723645..., which rounds to 7.72.
In a triangle with two unknown sides, x is found from the tangent ratio: tan 25° = x/7, so x = 7 × tan 25°.
In the same triangle, y is found from the cosine ratio: cos 25° = 7/y, so y = 7 / cos 25°.
If the lengths of two sides of a triangle are known, the angles can be calculated using trigonometric ratios.
When the opposite side and the adjacent side for the angle θ are known, use the tangent ratio.
Write the ratio of the known sides: with opposite 50 and adjacent 100, tan θ = 50/100.

The equation 3 sec α = 1.4 is converted to cosine form as 3 / cos α = 1.4.
After converting, rearrange the equation so that cos α is on one side of the equation.
From 3 / cos α = 1.4, multiplying both sides by cos α gives 3 = 1.4 cos α, and so 3 / 1.4 = cos α.

When a calculator error occurs because the ratio is out of range, write 'no solution' and not 'math error'.
When solving a trigonometric equation, an error from the calculator when calculating sin or cos means there is no solution to the equation.
Both the sine and cosine functions have a maximum value of 1.
To find the angle for a plotted point, draw a line from the origin to the point and draw a dotted line from the point to the x-axis, so that a right-angled triangle is constructed.
The coordinates of the point give the sides of the triangle: for P(2, 3), x = 2 and y = 3, so the side opposite angle A has length 3 and the adjacent side has length 2.
With the opposite side 3 and the adjacent side 2, use tan A = opposite/adjacent = 3/2 to calculate A = 56.3 degrees.
Alternatively, use the theorem of Pythagoras to calculate the hypotenuse of the triangle and then calculate the angle using sin A = opposite/hypotenuse or cos A = adjacent/hypotenuse.
The angle between the line from the origin to a point and the positive x-axis is said to be in the standard position of an angle (for Q(-2, 3), angle B is this angle).
Angles are always measured from the positive x-axis in an anti-clockwise direction.
For a point in the second quadrant such as Q(-2, 3), let alpha be the angle between line OQ and the negative x-axis, so that B + alpha = 180 degrees.
From the coordinates of Q(-2, 3), the side opposite alpha has length 3 and the adjacent side has length 2.
Use tan alpha = opposite/adjacent = 3/2 to calculate alpha = 56.3 degrees, then the angle in standard position is B = 180 degrees - alpha = 123.7 degrees.
Alternatively, calculate the hypotenuse using the theorem of Pythagoras and calculate alpha using sin alpha = opposite/hypotenuse or cos alpha = adjacent/hypotenuse.
The trigonometric ratios, first defined using right-angled triangles, extend to any angle; the definitions do not rely on the lengths of the sides of the triangle but on the size of the angle only.
The definitions of the reciprocal ratios (cosec, sec, cot) are extended to the Cartesian plane in the same way.
For a point P(x, y), a circle centred on the origin passing through P has radius r, which is the length from the origin to P.
The angle between line OP and the x-axis is denoted theta.
sin theta = y/r.
cosec theta = r/y.
cos theta = x/r.
sec theta = r/x.
tan theta = y/x.
cot theta = x/y.
To calculate the ratios for a point (x, y) without a calculator, use the theorem of Pythagoras to find r: r squared = x squared + y squared (for P(-3, 4), r squared = 25, so r = 5).
r is positive, as it is the radius of the circle.
After finding r, substitute the values of x, y and r into the required ratios (for P(-3, 4): x = -3, y = 4, r = 5).
For P(-3, 4), cos theta = x/r = -3/5.
The Cartesian plane is divided into 4 quadrants in an anti-clockwise direction.
r is always positive but x and y change with the position of the point, so the trigonometric ratios can be positive or negative.
The letters C, A, S and T on the diagram of the quadrants indicate which of the ratios are positive in each quadrant.
The diagram showing which ratios are positive in each quadrant is known as the CAST diagram.
Quadrant I: both x and y are positive, so all ratios are positive.
Quadrant II: y is positive, so sin and cosec are positive (they are defined in terms of y and r).
Quadrant III: both x and y are negative, so tan and cot are positive (they are defined in terms of x and y).
Quadrant IV: x is positive, so cos and sec are positive (they are defined in terms of x and r).
The hypotenuse, r, is a length, and is therefore always positive.
Whenever you have to solve trigonometric problems without a calculator, it can be very helpful to make a sketch.
Start by sketching the point in the Cartesian plane and labelling the angle.
To find a missing coordinate, rearrange the theorem of Pythagoras: y squared = r squared - x squared (for r = 13 and x = -5, y squared = 144, so y = plus or minus 12).
The quadrant decides the sign of the missing coordinate: given that theta lies in the third quadrant, y must be negative, so y = -12.
To evaluate an expression such as 3 tan theta, replace the ratio with its definition in x, y and r and simplify: for P(-3, 4), 3 tan theta = 3(y/x) = 3(4/-3) = -4.
To evaluate (1/2) cosec theta, replace cosec theta with r/y and simplify: for P(-3, 4), (1/2)(5/4) = 5/8.
For a squared ratio, substitute x, y and r into the definition and square it: tan squared theta + 1 = (y/x) squared + 1, which for x = -5, y = -12 gives 144/25 + 1 = 169/25.
The right-hand side is worked out separately: sec squared theta = (r/x) squared = (13/-5) squared = 169/25.
To prove an identity for the point, work out the left-hand side and the right-hand side separately; when they are equal, the identity is proved.
tan squared theta + 1 = sec squared theta; the book proves it by substituting x = -5, y = -12 and r = 13 for a point in the third quadrant.
When working in the Cartesian plane, two other special angles are included in right-angled triangles: 0 degrees and 90 degrees.
When theta = 0 degrees, the length of the opposite side is 0 and the length of the adjacent side equals the length of the hypotenuse.
sin 0 degrees = opposite/hypotenuse = 0/hypotenuse = 0.
cos 0 degrees = adjacent/hypotenuse = hypotenuse/hypotenuse = 1.
tan 0 degrees = opposite/adjacent = 0/adjacent = 0.
When theta = 90 degrees, the length of the adjacent side is 0 and the length of the opposite side equals the length of the hypotenuse.
sin 90 degrees = opposite/hypotenuse = hypotenuse/hypotenuse = 1.
cos 90 degrees = adjacent/hypotenuse = 0/hypotenuse = 0.
tan 90 degrees = opposite/adjacent = opposite/0, which is undefined.
Special angle values of sin theta for 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees: 0, 1/2, 1/sqrt2, sqrt3/2, 1.
Special angle values of cos theta for 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees: 1, sqrt3/2, 1/sqrt2, 1/2, 0.
Special angle values of tan theta for 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees: 0, 1/sqrt3, 1, sqrt3, undefined.
